UMN student’s death sparks community outcry

Following the death of 23-year-old student Fiqremariam “Kidus” Dereje Zewde at the end of September, family and community members are speaking out about the case and the impacts left behind.
Categories:
  • Campus
  • Campus Activities
  • Marquee
  • Student Life
  • Top Story
by Kyra Deters
Published November 23, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:50
Instaread

Having worked as the assistant project manager for the last few years at his father’s heating, ventilation and air conditioning company, Fiqremariam “Kidus” Dereje Zewde was set to become the organization’s lead project manager this year.

He was an altruistic and ambitious young man, Hawi Awash, Zewde’s aunt, said, dedicated to being a pillar of support for those around him. Zewde was also working towards a construction management degree at the University of Minnesota after finding his passion through working for his father during the summers.

On the night of Sept. 23, Zewde was found dead with a gunshot wound to the head, police told his family. 

He had parked his aunt’s car, which he drove that night, near the site of a Meta data center near the University’s Outreach, Research and Education Park, also known as UMore Park in Rosemount — less than 10 minutes away from his home. Rosemount Police Department Public Information Officer and Sergeant Alex Eckstein said officers were dispatched to the area around 11:30 p.m. for a welfare check following a 911 call, where they would eventually find Zewde’s body.

A devoted brother to his three younger siblings, Zewde had a strong attachment to his parents and family. Between hobbies and homework, Zewde regularly offered up bits of knowledge and passion to aid them on the journey to discovering their own.

“Kidus was extremely down to earth, always willing to lend a helping hand and very active in his family life,” Awash said. “He loves being hands-on and is a very resourceful guy.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Earlier that night, the TOCA Soccer and Sports Center in Burnsville hosted a match at around 8 p.m. Upon speaking with the center staff, Awash said staff confirmed that Zewde was among the 16 players signed up on the roster, and he was observed playing in the game on camera footage from that night.

Staff members told the family that during the match, Zewde collided with another player and took a break to rest. This has left family members questioning what occurred between the time he was seen at the game and when he was found.

Additionally, the medical examiner’s office informed the family that police said there was footage captured by the Meta data center prior to when Zewde was found. However, when Awash asked the police department about this footage, she received a conflicting response.

“The medical examiner’s office said there’s 30-minute footage from 11 to 11:30 — they are saying they found him at 11:31,” Awash said. “But then when I asked the police department, they said they don’t know anything about that, and they have not been able to retrieve any footage.”

If this footage does exist, Awash hopes that its possessors turn it over so she and her family can better understand what happened that night. She expressed her family’s skepticism regarding how Zewde was found, and the inconsistencies around it were reported to authorities by contractors near the area.

Mortenson Construction has been the main contractor for the Meta data center for the past two and a half years.

ADVERTISEMENT

“We were originally told that the security guards from the Meta center were the ones that found him, and then later the Meta center manager said it was not the security guard who found him,” Awash said. “But actually the Mortenson’s folks, even though the security guard from the data center was the one that called it in.”

Awash voiced her uncertainty surrounding this, and questioned why workers would have called the security company, rather than the police, upon finding her nephew.

Law enforcement officials arrived at Zewde’s residence around 3:13 a.m. to inform his parents of their son’s death, handing them a pair of keys and urging them to go pick up the car, according to Awash.

“That is how they were told,” Awash said. “They were shocked — and asked the police department to better their practices in terms of how they notify families when it comes to tragic situations such as this.”

Awash said the vehicle’s removal seemed to be the police department’s utmost priority that night because it was on the University’s private property near a newly constructed facility sold to Meta. The family found this to be strange, and it raised concerns about the quality and duration of the investigation despite the police department’s assurance that they collected all required evidence from the scene.

“Because it was a private property,” Awash said. “There was an urgency to move it, and I think our hesitation was very much like, did you secure the premises, did you do everything there was to do before asking us to move the vehicle?” 

ADVERTISEMENT

In an interview with the Minnesota Daily, Sergeant Alex Eckstein said he was not one of the responding officers. Although the case is still active, law enforcement officials have no suspicion that Zewde’s death had any homicidal involvement.

“At this time we don’t suspect foul play,” Eckstein said. “We don’t have anything that leads us to believe otherwise.”

Looking toward the future of the case, Eckstein acknowledged that this has been, and will continue to be, a difficult situation for all parties involved, including law enforcement officials and especially the family. He expressed the police department’s commitment to examining the events of that night in order to bring the case to a resolution.

The department will continue to work closely with the family and ensure they feel heard, he said. Eckstein added he knows members of Zewde’s family and the community want answers, and law enforcement officials will do what they can to provide insight into what happened that night.

Despite assurances, Awash said their family felt officials were too quick to label Zewde’s death as a suicide. This raised suspicion, and they are pursuing an independent autopsy.

“To us, they were very quick to tell us that it’s a suicide without doing any kind of [thorough] investigation, so that just really unsettled us,” Awash said. “We wanted to make sure that it was going to be fully investigated — the only way we can guarantee that is if we had an independent autopsy.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Police failed to retrieve any bullet or bullet fragments after bringing a canine and metal detector to the site, which flagged additional concerns, Awash said.

“My question with that is, where did the shell casing go from the gun? The shot happened, the shot casing falls down, so then did he get up and go move it?” Awash said. “Where did it go? That really doesn’t make sense.”

The University confirmed Zewde’s enrollment in the College of Liberal Arts between Fall 2021 and Spring 2026. They advise individuals in need of support during this time to contact the Office of Student Affairs’ Care Team, Boynton Mental Health or otherwise explore the University’s online resource tool, “Help Compass,” an anonymous crisis management resource.

“The death of a current or former student is a tragic loss for the University community,” the University wrote in a statement. “Resources are available to assist members of our community who are grieving.”

Katie Jackson, Dean of Students and associate vice president for Student Affairs, said the University has an annual event to honor students who have passed away during the past academic year. 

“Every year at the Northern Stars Student Remembrance, our University of Minnesota community comes together to honor the lives, legacies and lasting impact of the students we have lost, ensuring their memories remain an enduring part of our campus community,” Jackson said.

Awash said their family has received communications from the University, and Zewde will be included in this annual remembrance, which she expressed gratitude for.

However, this generosity did not suffice, Awash said.

The family requested to hold a vigil for Zewde in the location where he lost his life on the University-owned land near the outskirts of the Meta data center. They were denied access by the University due to liability concerns.

“I think that when a family is grieving, especially grieving one of your students as a school,” Awash said. “It’s crucial that you are able to extend those kinds of abilities to be able to host memorials or vigils like that on the property.”

University representatives say the liability concerns revolve around the location itself. The University’s Assistant Vice President for Planning, Space, and Real Estate Leslie Krueger visited the site on Oct. 3, identifying space and safety limitations with the capacity of the site.

“Staff took photos, provided a map of safety hazards to the family, and identified parking limitations. Due to the size of the family, it was determined that there wasn’t enough parking at the location to safely accommodate everyone at once,” the University said in a statement. “For this reason, the University offered to support the family in hosting the vigil at several alternative locations, including indoor and outdoor areas on campus, and to additionally honor Kidus at our annual Northern Stars Student Remembrance Event. The family chose not to host a vigil at the University campus, a decision we respect.”

To Awash, it is a significant shortcoming on behalf of the University. If empathy remains at the center of learning for students at institutions such as the University of Minnesota, she hopes to see change.

To bring justice to Zewde’s case, Awash said there is more that both the University and local law enforcement need to do. 

“It really is about amplifying, and I really do believe that advocating for our children is important, especially those who are voiceless and those who are not able to advocate for themselves,” Awash said. “I think that the University has a responsibility to advocate for its students — so it’s just helping amplify so that he does get a thorough and full investigation.”
